body.text: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be live streamed
In short:
The US says it will live stream its first firing squad execution by the military since World War II.
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who shot and killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, was sentenced to death in 2013.
What's next?
The execution is set to take place on December 3.
The United States's first execution by a military firing squad since World War II will be live streamed, the Pentagon has said.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people and injuring dozens more in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, would happen on December 3.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Mr Hegseth told conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice News.
"People need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things."
When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Mr Hegseth replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on December third."
The execution is set to take place at the Texas military base where Hasan committed his crimes.
The Pentagon official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not offer more information and said details would follow.

It comes days after US President Donald Trump approved the execution by firing squad, set to be the first execution carried out by the US military since 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was hanged.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist at the time of the Al-Qaeda inspired mass shooting, was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.
He chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges.
In November 2009, the US-born man opened fire at a medical facility on the Fort Hood base, which served as a staging point for soldiers later deployed to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Thirteen people were killed and 32 injured, most of them soldiers.
During Hasan's trial, it was revealed he spent weeks planning the deadly attack.

The court heard he videoed a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol he purchased, and went to a gun range outside Austin where he asked for advice on how to reload with speed and precision.
Soldiers later testified that Hasan's rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.
Mr Trump has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action.
Experts on military law said Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution.

"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," said Eugene R Fidell, a military law expert and visiting lecturer at Yale Law School.
Death penalty in spotlight after failed execution
This week authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched the execution of death row inmate Christa Pike, making headlines around the world.
Days after receiving two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, Pike woke up, becoming the first person to survive the administration of such drugs.
On Thursday, local time, Pike was walking around in her hospital room and speaking, according to her lawyer.
The botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner in which the US puts criminals to death.

Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and the vice-president of the National Institute of Military Justice, said at a time when many states were having difficulty carrying out lethal injections, firing squads were being seen as a more humane alternative.
"Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner," he said.
But Professor Fissell said: "I don't think that's what's motivating this [decision to execute Hasan by firing squad]."
"There's a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasise, the 'lethality culture'," he said.

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Mr Hegseth's announcement raised a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns about Hasan's dignity.
"This is a president who's about spectacle and that's, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver," Professor Semel said.
At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Last year, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.
